questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which statement best defines pharmacokinetics?

options.text: How the body absorbs, distributes, metabolises and eliminates a medicine.
What the medicine does to the body.
The classification of medicines by colour.

questions.rationale: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a medicine through absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which statement best defines pharmacodynamics?

options.text: How the medicine affects the body.
How the medicine is eliminated only.

questions.rationale: Pharmacodynamics describes the effects and mechanisms of a medicine in the body.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Why is the generic name of a medicine preferred in professional communication?

options.text: Brand names may differ between countries and manufacturers.
It replaces the need for checking the label.

questions.rationale: Generic names support consistent communication because brand names vary across manufacturers and countries.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A medicine intended to reduce pain is classified as which type?
questions.rationale: Analgesics are medicines used to relieve pain.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A patient with impaired kidney function is prescribed a medicine mainly eliminated by the kidneys. What is the nurse's main concern?

options.text: The medicine may accumulate and cause toxicity.
The medicine may be absorbed too quickly.
The medicine will have no therapeutic effect.
The medicine will become an antibiotic.

questions.rationale: Reduced renal elimination can cause accumulation and increase the risk of toxicity.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A medicine produces the intended reduction in blood pressure. This is called the:
questions.rationale: The therapeutic effect is the intended beneficial action of a medicine.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A patient develops mild predictable drowsiness after an antihistamine. This is best described as a:
questions.rationale: A side effect is a predictable secondary effect that may occur alongside the intended action.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which factor can alter medication metabolism?
questions.rationale: The liver is a major site of medication metabolism, so impaired function may alter medicine levels.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A nurse checks blood pressure and electrolytes before giving a diuretic. What principle is being applied?

options.text: Pharmacological knowledge linked to patient assessment.

questions.rationale: The nurse is using knowledge of expected effects and risks to guide safe assessment before administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which medicine class is commonly used to reduce blood clot formation?
questions.rationale: Anticoagulants reduce the formation or extension of blood clots.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A patient develops unexpected severe bleeding after a medicine. This is best classified as:
questions.rationale: Severe bleeding is a harmful unwanted effect requiring assessment and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Why should a nurse know the main purpose of every medicine administered?

options.text: To recognise whether the treatment is effective and identify risks.

questions.rationale: Knowing the indication helps the nurse assess therapeutic response and detect adverse effects.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A patient is dehydrated and receives a medicine cleared by the kidneys. Why is this clinically important?

options.text: Dehydration may alter renal perfusion and medicine elimination.

questions.rationale: Dehydration can reduce renal perfusion and alter elimination, increasing risk of accumulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which description best distinguishes an adverse reaction from a side effect?

options.text: An adverse reaction may be harmful or unexpected, while a side effect is often predictable.
A side effect is always life-threatening.
Adverse reactions occur only with injections.

questions.rationale: Adverse reactions may be harmful or unexpected, while side effects are often known secondary effects.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A medicine stimulates a receptor and increases heart rate. This is an example of:
questions.rationale: The medicine's action on a receptor and resulting physiological change are pharmacodynamic effects.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which patient is at greatest risk of medicine accumulation?

options.text: A healthy adult with normal organ function.
A patient receiving a topical cream.
An older adult with severe kidney impairment.

questions.rationale: Severe kidney impairment can reduce elimination and increase accumulation risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A nurse notices that a patient has not improved after several doses of an antibiotic. What is the BEST nursing action?

options.text: Assess the patient and report lack of therapeutic response.

questions.rationale: The nurse should evaluate effectiveness and escalate concerns rather than changing treatment independently.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which statement about route of administration is correct?

options.text: Route has no effect on a medicine.
Route can influence absorption and onset of action.
All routes are equally safe for every patient.
The patient always chooses the route.

questions.rationale: Different routes affect how quickly and reliably a medicine is absorbed and whether it is appropriate for the patient.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: A patient has a serious allergy to a medicine class. Why is this information essential?

options.text: It may represent a contraindication to related medicines.

questions.rationale: A previous serious allergy may make related medicines unsafe and requires careful checking.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Pharmacology and Medication Safety
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates sound pharmacological nursing practice?

options.text: The medicine was given on time only.
The patient recognised the tablet colour.
The nurse understood the indication, assessed risks, administered safely and evaluated the response.

questions.rationale: Safe pharmacological practice integrates knowledge, assessment, administration and evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Before administering any medicine, the nurse should FIRST:

options.text: Confirm the patient's identity using approved identifiers.

questions.rationale: Correct patient identification is a fundamental safety check before medicine administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A prescription requires 500 mg. The medicine available is 250 mg in 5 mL. How many millilitres are required?
questions.rationale: Required dose divided by available dose multiplied by volume: 500/250 × 5 = 10 mL.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Which action best reflects the right route?

options.text: Using the route preferred by the nurse.
Giving the medicine by the prescribed route after confirming it is appropriate.

questions.rationale: The route must match the valid order and be clinically appropriate.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A medication label is unclear. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Administer it if the colour is familiar.
Ask the patient to identify it.
Write a new label from memory.
Do not use it and obtain a clearly labelled product.

questions.rationale: Unclear or unlabelled medicines should never be administered.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Why should medicines be prepared for one patient at a time?

options.text: To reduce the risk of patient and medicine selection errors.
To avoid using a medication trolley.

questions.rationale: Preparing one patient's medicines at a time supports accurate identification and reduces mix-ups.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A nurse is interrupted during a medication calculation. What is the safest response?

options.text: Restart or recheck the calculation before proceeding.
Ask the patient to calculate it.

questions.rationale: Interruptions can disrupt concentration; calculations should be rechecked before administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Which item must be checked before using a medication vial?
questions.rationale: Expiry and product integrity are essential to safe medication preparation.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A patient is unable to swallow safely. An oral tablet is prescribed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the family to give it.
Assess and clarify the route before administration.

questions.rationale: The route may be unsafe; the nurse should assess and clarify an alternative.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Which statement about dose calculations is MOST accurate?

options.text: A mathematically correct answer should also be checked for reasonableness.
Calculators remove the need for checking.

questions.rationale: A result should be clinically reasonable and use correct units, especially where decimals are involved.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A nurse prepares an injection but cannot remember whether a second check is required. What should happen?

options.text: Proceed because the dose is small.
Review the policy and obtain the required check before administration.

questions.rationale: The nurse should follow organisational policy for independent checks.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Which medication right involves assessing whether the medicine is appropriate for the patient's current condition?
questions.rationale: The right assessment requires relevant clinical checks before administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A prescription is written as .5 mg. Why should the nurse seek clarification?

options.text: The dose is always too low.
The route is missing from all prescriptions.
A leading zero is missing and the decimal may be misread.

questions.rationale: Writing 0.5 mg reduces the risk of a tenfold error from a missed decimal point.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A patient says the tablet looks different from usual. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Pause, verify the medicine against the order and packaging.

questions.rationale: Patient concerns can identify errors and should prompt verification.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A medicine is ordered intravenously, but the nurse has not been assessed as competent in IV administration. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Seek an appropriately competent nurse or supervision.
Ask the patient for consent to proceed.

questions.rationale: Nurses must practise within competence and organisational requirements.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A child weighs 20 kg and is prescribed 5 mg/kg. What dose is required?
questions.rationale: 5 mg × 20 kg = 100 mg.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Which action best supports aseptic medication preparation?

options.text: Touching key parts with bare hands.
Preparing in a clean area with minimal interruption.

questions.rationale: A clean preparation area and protection of key parts reduce contamination risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A patient refuses a scheduled medicine. Which right is being exercised?
questions.rationale: A competent patient has the right to refuse treatment after receiving appropriate information.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A nurse documents a medicine before administration. Why is this unsafe?

options.text: The record may become inaccurate if the medicine is delayed, refused or not given.
It is only unsafe for injections.

questions.rationale: Documentation must reflect actual care provided.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: A sublingual medicine is prescribed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Place it under the tongue as ordered and explain not to swallow immediately.

questions.rationale: Sublingual medicines are placed under the tongue for absorption through the mucosa.

questions.sectionLabel: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates safe administration?

options.text: The medicine was removed from storage.
The nurse completed the round quickly.
The correct patient received the correct medicine, dose, route and time, with documentation and evaluation.

questions.rationale: Safe administration includes deliberate checks, correct delivery, documentation and monitoring.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient develops facial swelling and difficulty breathing after an antibiotic. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.text: Stop the medicine and call for emergency assistance.

questions.rationale: Facial swelling and breathing difficulty may indicate anaphylaxis and require immediate emergency response.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Which factor commonly contributes to medication errors?
questions.rationale: Look-alike packaging can contribute to wrong-medicine selection errors.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A contraindication is best described as:

options.text: A reason a medicine may be unsuitable or unsafe.

questions.rationale: A contraindication is a condition or factor that makes use of a medicine inappropriate or risky.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient takes a prescribed medicine and an herbal product. Why should the nurse ask about both?

options.text: The information is not clinically relevant.
Herbal products may interact with medicines.

questions.rationale: Herbal and complementary products may cause interactions and adverse effects.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient develops mild nausea after a medicine known to cause nausea. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess severity and monitor while providing appropriate care.

questions.rationale: Known side effects still require assessment and management, but they are not automatically allergies.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests an allergic reaction?
questions.rationale: Rash, wheeze and swelling are typical features of an immune-mediated allergic reaction.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A medication error is discovered before the medicine reaches the patient. What should happen?

options.text: Report the near miss according to policy.

questions.rationale: Near misses reveal system risks and should be reported for learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient has severe kidney impairment. Which risk should be considered before administering a renally cleared medicine?
questions.rationale: Impaired renal clearance may cause medicine accumulation and toxicity.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient develops severe bleeding while taking an anticoagulant. What is the BEST action?
questions.rationale: Severe bleeding is a serious adverse reaction requiring prompt assessment and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Why should allergy information be updated after a serious reaction?
questions.rationale: Clear allergy documentation protects the patient from receiving the medicine again.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Which situation represents duplicate therapy?

options.text: A medicine is given at the correct time.
Two medicines from the same class are prescribed unintentionally for the same purpose.

questions.rationale: Duplicate therapy can increase adverse effects and may represent a prescribing or reconciliation error.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A nurse notices two patients with similar names and similar medication profiles. What is the BEST prevention strategy?

options.text: Ask the patients to exchange information.

questions.rationale: Consistent use of approved identifiers prevents wrong-patient errors.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient develops confusion and low blood pressure after a new medicine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess for an adverse reaction and escalate as required.

questions.rationale: New confusion and hypotension may indicate a serious adverse effect and require prompt assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Which action best reduces interruption-related medication errors?

options.text: Preparing several patients' medicines at once.
Creating a protected preparation process and repeating checks after interruption.

questions.rationale: Reducing interruptions and restarting checks when disrupted improves safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient has a documented anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. A related antibiotic is prescribed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Administer because it is a different brand.
Ask the patient to try one dose.
Hold and clarify the order before administration.

questions.rationale: A serious allergy may contraindicate related medicines and requires clarification.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A nurse administers the wrong dose, but the patient appears well. What is the FIRST priority?

options.text: Assess the patient and seek appropriate clinical review.

questions.rationale: Immediate assessment and treatment take priority even if no harm is initially apparent.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes an interaction from an allergy?

options.text: An interaction occurs when one substance alters another medicine's effect; an allergy is an immune response.

questions.rationale: Interactions and allergies are different mechanisms and require different assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin begins a new herbal supplement and develops bruising. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Some herbal products may increase bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulants.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Why should errors not be concealed?

options.text: Concealment prevents timely treatment and system learning.

questions.rationale: Open reporting supports patient safety, appropriate treatment and prevention of recurrence.

questions.sectionLabel: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective response to a serious medication reaction?

options.text: The medicine was stopped, the patient treated, the reaction documented and future re-exposure prevented.

questions.rationale: Effective response includes immediate care, documentation, communication and prevention.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A prescriber's order appears unsafe. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give it because it is prescribed.

questions.rationale: The nurse remains accountable for questioning unclear or unsafe orders.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: When should medication administration be documented?

options.text: At the end of the week.

questions.rationale: Documentation should reflect actual care and be completed promptly after administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A competent patient refuses a medicine. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.text: Explore the patient's concerns and provide information.

questions.rationale: The nurse should understand the reason, provide education and respect informed refusal.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Which information should patient medication education include?

options.text: Name, purpose, dose, timing, important side effects and when to seek help.

questions.rationale: Effective education includes practical information needed for safe use.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: What is teach-back?

options.text: Asking the patient to explain the instructions in their own words.
Repeating the same information more loudly.

questions.rationale: Teach-back confirms whether the explanation was effective.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient refuses an anticoagulant because of fear of bleeding. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Explain benefits and risks, answer questions and notify the appropriate clinician if refusal continues.
Ask another patient to persuade them.

questions.rationale: The nurse should support informed decision-making and respect refusal.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Which documentation entry is MOST appropriate after a refused dose?

options.text: 'Dose refused; patient stated concern about nausea; education provided and prescriber notified.'

questions.rationale: Objective documentation should record the refusal, reason, education and follow-up.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A nurse realises a dose was omitted earlier. What should happen?

options.text: Assess the patient, notify appropriately and document the omission honestly.

questions.rationale: Omissions require assessment, communication and transparent documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates accountability?

options.text: Seeking clarification when unsure and accepting responsibility for actions.
Relying on the prescriber for all decisions.

questions.rationale: Professional accountability includes safe judgement, clarification and honesty.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Why should patients be taught not to double a missed dose unless instructed?

options.text: Doubling may cause overdose or harm.

questions.rationale: Taking extra medicine may produce toxicity or serious adverse effects.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient cannot read the medication leaflet. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Ask the patient to sign anyway.
Provide plain-language verbal teaching, visual support and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Education should be adapted to health literacy and understanding confirmed.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient asks whether alcohol interacts with a new medicine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give accurate medicine-specific guidance or seek clarification from pharmacy/prescriber.

questions.rationale: Patient education should be accurate and tailored to the medicine.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient reports using medicines from two doctors and over-the-counter products. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review the complete medication list for duplication and interaction risks.
Ask the patient to stop everything.

questions.rationale: A complete medication history supports safe education and reconciliation.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A nurse is asked to administer a medicine outside their scope of competence. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Seek supervision or an appropriately competent practitioner.

questions.rationale: Nurses must practise within competence and obtain support where needed.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient demonstrates incorrect inhaler technique after teaching. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to read the label.
Repeat and adapt teaching, then reassess technique.

questions.rationale: Education should continue until the patient can use the medicine safely.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Which entry best documents a PRN analgesic?

options.text: Drug, dose, route, time, indication and response.

questions.rationale: PRN medication documentation should include the indication and evaluation of effect.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient requests to stop a medicine because of side effects. What is the BEST nursing action?

options.text: Assess the symptoms, provide information and involve the prescriber before changes.
Tell the patient to stop immediately.

questions.rationale: The nurse should assess, educate and coordinate safe review rather than independently changing treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Which approach best supports adherence?

options.text: Understanding the patient's concerns and simplifying the plan where clinically possible.

questions.rationale: Adherence improves when education and plans address individual barriers.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: A patient asks why the nurse is checking identity again. What is the BEST response?
questions.rationale: Explaining the safety purpose promotes trust and patient participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe and accountable medication education?

options.text: The patient accurately explains the medicine plan, risks and when to seek help.

questions.rationale: Understanding is demonstrated when the patient can explain the plan correctly.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: An IQN is unfamiliar with the local controlled-drug register. What is the BEST action before administering a controlled medicine?

options.text: Request orientation and follow the local controlled-drug policy with supervision.
Ask a colleague to sign later.

questions.rationale: Local controlled-drug processes must be understood and followed before independent practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Which information makes a medication order valid and complete?

options.text: Patient name and medicine colour only.
Patient, medicine, dose, route, timing and authorised prescriber.

questions.rationale: A valid order clearly identifies the patient, medicine, dose, route, timing and prescriber.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: An electronic record displays an allergy alert that the patient says is incorrect. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Verify the allergy history and clarify the record before administration.
Administer because the patient denies it.

questions.rationale: Electronic alerts support but do not replace verification and clinical judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A prescription reads “.5 mg” of a high-risk medicine. What is the safest response?

options.text: Clarify the dose because the missing leading zero creates error risk.

questions.rationale: A leading zero should be used for doses below one to prevent tenfold errors.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates safe adaptation to an unfamiliar eMAR?

options.text: Completing supervised orientation and confirming competence before independent use.

questions.rationale: Orientation and competency confirmation are essential when systems are unfamiliar.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: What is a major risk of electronic medication systems?

options.text: Wrong-patient selection or copying outdated information.

questions.rationale: Electronic systems can introduce selection, copying and alert-fatigue risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A verbal order is received in a noisy emergency area. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Ask a family member to confirm.
Use read-back and document according to policy.

questions.rationale: Read-back reduces communication error with verbal orders.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: An IQN knows the generic medicine but not the local brand. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the patient to identify it.
Confirm the generic name, formulation and order before administration.

questions.rationale: Brand names differ; verification should focus on the generic medicine and formulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A system alert is repeatedly overridden by staff. What safety concern does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Frequent low-value alerts may lead to alert fatigue and unsafe overrides.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Which action is within professional accountability?

options.text: Administering an unclear order because it is signed.
Questioning and clarifying an unsafe or incomplete order.
Letting the prescriber assume all responsibility.

questions.rationale: Nurses remain accountable for safe medication decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A medication chart uses an abbreviation unfamiliar to the IQN. What should happen?
questions.rationale: Unfamiliar or ambiguous abbreviations must be clarified.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A nurse selects the correct patient but the wrong episode of care in the eMAR. What is the primary risk?

options.text: The patient will be discharged early.
No risk exists if the name matches.
Incorrect or outdated medication information may be used.

questions.rationale: Selecting the wrong encounter can expose outdated or irrelevant orders.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Which process best supports controlled-drug accountability?

options.text: Required witnessing, secure storage and accurate register entries.
Documenting at the end of the week.

questions.rationale: Controlled medicines require strict storage, witnessing and documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A nurse is unsure whether local policy requires an independent check. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed because the dose is familiar.
Check the policy and obtain the required verification.

questions.rationale: Policy should be confirmed before proceeding.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Why should nurses not rely solely on barcode scanning?

options.text: Technology may fail or contain incorrect data.

questions.rationale: Technology supports, but does not replace, clinical and identity checks.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Which outcome best shows safe transition into a new medication system?

options.text: The nurse delegates all medication work.
The nurse follows local processes consistently and uses clinical judgement.

questions.rationale: Safe transition combines local system competence with professional judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A nurse notices an electronic default dose is inconsistent with the patient’s order. What should happen?

options.text: Ask the patient to select the dose.

questions.rationale: Default settings can create errors and must be checked against the valid order.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: A colleague offers their password so the IQN can enter the eMAR. What is the correct response?

options.text: Decline and access the system only through authorised credentials.

questions.rationale: Passwords are personal and access must be authorised and traceable.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: Which practice most reduces prescribing-interpretation risk?
questions.rationale: Ambiguous orders should be clarified before administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Applying International Medication Safety Standards
questions.stem: What is the BEST indicator of medication-system competence?

options.text: Accurate use of local charts, alerts, checks and escalation processes.

questions.rationale: Competence is demonstrated through accurate, safe use of the entire medication process.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Which medicine is commonly considered high-risk?
questions.rationale: Insulin can cause serious harm if dose, timing or monitoring are incorrect.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient prescribed insulin has a blood glucose of 2.8 mmol/L. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Treat hypoglycaemia and follow escalation policy before the dose.

questions.rationale: Hypoglycaemia requires immediate treatment and review before insulin administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: What makes an independent double check meaningful?

options.text: Each clinician verifies separately before comparing results.

questions.rationale: Independent verification reduces shared-assumption errors.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient receiving an opioid has a respiratory rate of 8/min. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Withhold according to policy, assess urgently and escalate.

questions.rationale: Respiratory depression is a serious opioid-related risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient on anticoagulants has new bruising and a markedly abnormal coagulation result. What is the priority?

options.text: Withhold according to policy, assess for bleeding and notify the team.

questions.rationale: Abnormal coagulation with bruising signals increased bleeding risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Which result is most relevant before giving a potassium-containing medicine?
questions.rationale: Electrolyte and renal status directly affect safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A chemotherapy dose is prescribed. Which additional safeguard is most appropriate?
questions.rationale: Chemotherapy is high-risk and requires protocol-based safeguards.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A sedative is due, but the patient is newly confused and unsteady. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassess and seek review before administration.

questions.rationale: Current condition must be linked to each dose.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Which patient factor most influences opioid safety?

options.text: Respiratory rate and level of sedation.

questions.rationale: Respiratory and sedation assessment are essential before opioids.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient on digoxin has a very low pulse. What is the safest response?

options.text: Withhold according to policy and seek review.

questions.rationale: Bradycardia may indicate increased risk and requires review.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A concentrated electrolyte ampoule is found in an unrestricted medication drawer. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Remove and report according to high-risk storage policy.
Ask patients not to touch it.

questions.rationale: Concentrated electrolytes require restricted, controlled storage.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Why are standard concentrations used for IV infusions?

options.text: To reduce calculation and preparation variability.

questions.rationale: Standardisation reduces dosing and preparation errors.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient’s renal function has deteriorated before a renally cleared medicine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review the result and clarify whether the dose remains appropriate.

questions.rationale: Renal deterioration may require dose adjustment or withholding.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A high-risk medicine requires a second check, but no authorised checker is available. What should happen?

options.text: Delay safely and escalate for an authorised checker.

questions.rationale: The required safeguard should not be bypassed.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Which finding is most important before anticoagulant administration?

options.text: Evidence of bleeding and relevant coagulation results.

questions.rationale: Bleeding assessment and coagulation data guide safe administration.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient’s potassium is critically high and a potassium supplement is due. What is the priority?
questions.rationale: Critically high potassium makes supplementation unsafe.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s role in therapeutic monitoring?

options.text: Know relevant tests and act on abnormal results.

questions.rationale: Nurses must connect monitoring data to medication decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: A patient receiving insulin is fasting unexpectedly. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the usual dose without review.
Assess blood glucose and clarify the plan.
Ask the patient to eat secretly.

questions.rationale: Fasting alters insulin risk and requires assessment and review.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Which statement best describes high-risk medicine practice?

options.text: Use additional safeguards because errors may cause serious harm.

questions.rationale: Additional safeguards reduce severe harm from high-risk medicines.

questions.sectionLabel: Clinical Pharmacology and High-Risk Medicines
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates safe high-risk medication management?

options.text: The dose was given on time.
The order, patient data, independent checks and monitoring were all integrated before and after administration.

questions.rationale: Safe practice integrates multiple safeguards and clinical data.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: What is the purpose of medication reconciliation?

options.text: To compare what the patient was actually taking with current orders.

questions.rationale: Reconciliation identifies omissions, duplication and discrepancies.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Which items should be included in a medication history?
questions.rationale: A complete history includes all relevant products and allergies.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A home anticoagulant is missing from the admission chart. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Verify the history and notify the prescriber promptly.

questions.rationale: Discrepancies must be clarified and resolved.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Why are transitions of care high-risk?

options.text: Medication lists may be incomplete or inconsistent.

questions.rationale: Transitions create risk of omissions, duplication and confusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Which ISBAR statement is most effective?

options.text: “Mr Lee’s warfarin is missing from the admission chart; he took it yesterday. Please review urgently before the next dose.”

questions.rationale: Clear communication identifies the patient, issue, evidence and requested action.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: After a medication error, what is the FIRST priority?
questions.rationale: Immediate patient care comes first.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: What should an incident report contain?
questions.rationale: Incident reports should support objective learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A discharge list contains both the old and new dose of the same medicine. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Clarify and correct the discrepancy before discharge.

questions.rationale: Duplicate or conflicting instructions must be resolved.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A patient reports taking an herbal supplement not listed in the chart. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Add it to the medication history and assess interaction risk.
Tell the patient to stop immediately.

questions.rationale: Complementary products may interact and belong in reconciliation.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A near miss occurs because two medicines have similar packaging. What should follow?

options.text: No action because no harm occurred.
Report the near miss and identify system factors.

questions.rationale: Near misses reveal system weaknesses.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Which documentation best supports a medication incident review?

options.text: Objective timeline of assessment, actions, response and notifications.

questions.rationale: A clear factual timeline supports continuity and review.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A patient transfers wards with an incomplete medication list. What should the receiving nurse do?

options.text: Use the previous list without question.
Ask the patient to remember doses later.
Reconcile and clarify discrepancies before administration.

questions.rationale: Transfer is a high-risk point requiring reconciliation.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Which discrepancy is most urgent?

options.text: A missing high-risk anticoagulant due soon.

questions.rationale: Missing a high-risk medicine can cause immediate harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A patient cannot recall doses. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use multiple reliable sources such as pharmacy, records and carers with consent.

questions.rationale: Medication histories should be verified using reliable sources.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Why should incident reports avoid blame?

options.text: Blame discourages reporting and hides system causes.

questions.rationale: A learning approach examines contributing factors while preserving fair accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A prescriber does not respond to an urgent medication discrepancy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Escalate through the next approved pathway.

questions.rationale: Escalation should continue when urgency is not matched by response.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Which outcome best shows effective medication reconciliation?

options.text: Discrepancies were identified, clarified, documented and communicated.

questions.rationale: Effective reconciliation resolves discrepancies and communicates the final plan.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: A medication omission is discovered after transfer. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Assess the patient and notify the appropriate clinician.

questions.rationale: Patient assessment and timely review are required.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: Which communication approach best supports closed-loop safety?

options.text: State the message, have it repeated back and confirm accuracy.

questions.rationale: Closed-loop communication confirms that critical information was received correctly.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management
questions.stem: What is the best indicator of professional incident management?

options.text: The patient is protected, facts are documented, relevant people are informed and system learning follows.

questions.rationale: Professional management combines immediate care, communication and learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient with limited English is learning insulin injection. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Use a professional interpreter, demonstration and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Interpreter support and demonstration improve safety and understanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: What does teach-back assess?
questions.rationale: Teach-back checks the clarity of education.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient fasts for religious reasons while taking diabetes medicine. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the patient to stop fasting.
Explore the plan respectfully and coordinate safe medication timing.

questions.rationale: Culturally responsive care balances beliefs with safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which statement best supports shared decision-making?

options.text: “There is no need to ask questions.”
“These are the options, benefits and risks; what matters most to you?”

questions.rationale: Shared decision-making includes informed options and patient preferences.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient cannot understand a complex dosing schedule. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use plain language, visual schedules and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Education should be adapted to health literacy.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Why should nurses ask about traditional medicines?

options.text: They may influence adherence or interact with prescribed medicines.

questions.rationale: Traditional and complementary products may affect safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient demonstrates incorrect inhaler technique after teaching. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Repeat and adapt education, then reassess technique.

questions.rationale: Education should continue until safe technique is demonstrated.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which topic is important when teaching a new sedating medicine?
questions.rationale: Sedation can affect driving and interact with alcohol.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient refuses a medicine because of fear of dependence. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore the concern and provide balanced information.

questions.rationale: Respectful enquiry supports informed decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which outcome best shows successful medication education?

options.text: The patient accurately explains and demonstrates the plan.
The nurse spoke for ten minutes.

questions.rationale: Understanding is shown through accurate explanation or demonstration.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient with low vision needs a complex medicine schedule. What is the BEST intervention?

options.text: Large-print or accessible labels, organised schedule and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Education should be adapted to sensory needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient asks whether to double a missed dose. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide medicine-specific guidance and discourage doubling unless instructed.

questions.rationale: Missed-dose advice must be safe and specific.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient cannot afford one prescribed medicine. What is the BEST nursing response?

options.text: Explore the barrier and involve the team in affordable safe options.
Tell the patient to stop all medicines.

questions.rationale: Practical barriers should be addressed through coordinated care.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which action best supports culturally safe education?

options.text: Ask rather than assume beliefs and preferences.
Provide identical teaching regardless of need.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety requires respectful individual enquiry.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient is being discharged with warfarin. Which education is most important?

options.text: Bleeding signs, monitoring, interactions and when to seek help.

questions.rationale: Warfarin requires monitoring and bleeding-risk education.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient on insulin cannot demonstrate hypoglycaemia management. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the patient to read later.
Continue education and correct the gap before discharge.

questions.rationale: Critical self-management skills should be confirmed before discharge.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects adherence support?

options.text: Explore barriers and agree on a realistic plan.

questions.rationale: Adherence improves when individual barriers are addressed.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient uses alcohol daily and is prescribed a medicine with interaction risk. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess use non-judgementally and provide specific safety advice.
Tell the patient never to disclose alcohol use.

questions.rationale: Non-judgemental assessment supports accurate risk management.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: A patient with cognitive impairment needs medication education. What is the BEST plan?

options.text: Use simple repeated information, assess capacity and involve appropriate support.

questions.rationale: Education should be adapted while preserving participation and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which outcome best represents person-centred medication safety?

options.text: The patient understands, participates and can manage the treatment safely.

questions.rationale: Person-centred safety combines understanding, participation and safe self-management.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which statement best describes medication governance?

options.text: A system of oversight covering selection, storage, prescribing, preparation, administration, monitoring and review of medicines.
A process limited to ordering pharmacy stock.
A nursing checklist used only at the bedside.
A financial system for medicine purchasing.

questions.rationale: Medication governance provides organisational oversight across the full medication-use process, supported by policy, committees, audits, credentialing and incident systems.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A junior nurse reports selecting the wrong infusion concentration before it reached the patient. What is the BEST leadership response?

options.text: Confirm patient safety, thank the nurse for reporting and review both individual learning and system factors.
Ignore the event because no harm occurred.
Remove the nurse permanently from medication duties.

questions.rationale: A just and learning-oriented response protects the patient, supports reporting and examines training, storage, labelling, workload and workflow.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which leader behaviour most strongly supports a positive medication-safety culture?

options.text: Expecting staff to manage uncertainty privately.
Encouraging staff to clarify unusual doses and report near misses.
Focusing only on completed medication rounds.

questions.rationale: A positive culture makes questioning, stopping and reporting normal and safe.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A nurse repeatedly bypasses an independent check because the process is inconvenient, despite coaching and clear warnings. Which just-culture category is MOST relevant?
questions.rationale: Repeatedly choosing a shortcut while underestimating risk is generally at-risk behaviour and calls for coaching, removal of incentives for shortcuts and proportionate accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A nurse administers a medicine incorrectly after selecting the wrong item from two almost identical packages. Which response best reflects systems thinking?

options.text: Review packaging, storage, labelling, workflow, interruptions and training.
Focus only on the nurse's final action.
Replace the nurse without changing the system.

questions.rationale: Medication harm often results from interacting system conditions rather than one action alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which governance activity best confirms continuing medication competence?

options.text: Supervised practice, formal assessment and periodic review.

questions.rationale: Medication competence should be supported by education, supervised practice, assessment and periodic review.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A senior clinician dismisses a nurse's concern about an unusual opioid dose because of hierarchy. What should the nurse leader do?

options.text: Tell the nurse to follow the senior clinician.
Delay review until the next meeting.
Reinforce that concerns should be raised regardless of hierarchy and ensure the order is reviewed.

questions.rationale: Leaders must ensure hierarchy does not silence medication-safety concerns and should support timely review.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST indicates that medication governance is functioning effectively?

options.text: Policies exist but are rarely used.
Staff can access guidance, report concerns, demonstrate competence and receive feedback from audits.

questions.rationale: Effective governance is visible in accessible guidance, competent practice, transparent reporting and monitored improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A nurse makes a one-time calculation slip in a poorly designed electronic form and reports it immediately. Which response is most consistent with just culture?

options.text: Support the nurse and redesign the form while addressing learning needs.

questions.rationale: A human error should prompt support and system redesign while still ensuring competence and learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which leadership action best strengthens medication accountability without creating fear?

options.text: Apply the same punishment to every incident.
Use fair review based on behaviour, context and risk.

questions.rationale: Fair, proportionate review supports accountability while preserving openness and trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A medication committee notices repeated insulin incidents. What should it do FIRST?

options.text: Review incident patterns, current processes and contributing conditions.

questions.rationale: Governance decisions should begin with analysis of data and current practice before selecting interventions.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects professional accountability in advanced medication practice?

options.text: Using judgement, questioning unsafe practice and accepting responsibility for decisions.

questions.rationale: Advanced accountability includes clinical judgement, speaking up and ownership of professional decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A new infusion policy is introduced but staff lack training and equipment. What is the primary governance failure?

options.text: The organisation did not align policy with implementation resources.
The policy should not be monitored.

questions.rationale: Policies require staffing, equipment, education and implementation support to become reliable practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which activity is most appropriate for an experienced nurse mentor?

options.text: Coach, observe practice and provide constructive feedback linked to standards.
Complete medication tasks for junior staff indefinitely.

questions.rationale: Mentoring should build competence through coaching, supervised practice and feedback.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A nurse leader thanks staff for reporting incidents but never follows up. What is the likely consequence?
questions.rationale: Staff notice when leadership messages are not matched by action; failure to follow through weakens trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which factor most clearly demonstrates psychological safety in medication practice?

options.text: Staff avoid questions to appear competent.
Staff admit uncertainty before administering a medicine.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety allows people to ask questions, admit uncertainty and speak up early.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: An experienced nurse intentionally overrides a critical safety control for convenience after repeated warnings. What response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Proportionate accountability alongside review of contributing factors.
No action because the nurse is experienced.

questions.rationale: Reckless disregard requires fair accountability, while organisations should still examine system conditions.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which metric would best support governance oversight of controlled-drug practice?

options.text: Audit findings, discrepancies, incident trends and competency compliance.

questions.rationale: Governance oversight should use relevant quality, safety and competence indicators.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: A medication-safety policy is consistently bypassed because it adds unnecessary duplication. What should the leader do?

options.text: Remove the policy immediately without approval.
Investigate workflow, redesign the process safely and monitor the change.

questions.rationale: Persistent workarounds are safety signals and may indicate poor process design that requires structured review.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Medication Safety and Clinical Governance
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST reflects mature medication-safety leadership?

options.text: Incidents are hidden to protect reputation.
Staff report risks, leaders respond fairly, competence is monitored and improvements are sustained.

questions.rationale: Mature leadership combines openness, fair accountability, competence assurance and sustained system improvement.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Why are reminders alone often weak medication-safety controls?

options.text: They rely heavily on memory and attention.

questions.rationale: Education and reminders depend on human attention and are less reliable than stronger system controls.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which intervention is strongest in the hierarchy of controls for look-alike medicines?

options.text: Separate storage and redesign packaging or selection systems.
Ask staff to be more careful.

questions.rationale: Removing or redesigning the hazard is stronger than relying on awareness alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A ward has repeated wrong-drug selection involving adjacent storage. What should the review examine?

options.text: Storage, labelling, electronic search design, interruptions and workflow.

questions.rationale: Systems thinking examines the full medication process and interacting contributory factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which human factor most directly increases risk during medication preparation?
questions.rationale: Interruptions disrupt attention and working memory, increasing error risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: What is a forcing function?

options.text: A design feature that makes an unsafe action impossible or difficult.

questions.rationale: Forcing functions physically or electronically prevent or constrain unsafe choices.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A smart pump allows a dangerously high dose because the drug library is outdated. What type of contributing factor is this?
questions.rationale: Outdated safety limits reflect technology maintenance and governance weaknesses.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which review question best reflects systems thinking?

options.text: What conditions made the error possible?
How quickly can staff be retrained?

questions.rationale: Systems thinking seeks the conditions and interactions that shaped the event.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A nurse chooses the wrong medicine from a cluttered screen. Which redesign is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Improve name display, differentiation and search results.

questions.rationale: Interface redesign addresses the selection hazard directly and is stronger than reminders.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which recommendation is least useful after an incident review?
questions.rationale: General instructions are not specific, measurable or reliable controls.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A review identifies fatigue and understaffing during night shifts. Which response best addresses the risk?

options.text: Review staffing, workload and medication timing while monitoring outcomes.
Require staff to sign a pledge.

questions.rationale: Workload and staffing are system factors that require operational redesign and evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which measure best tests whether separated storage reduced selection errors?

options.text: Wrong-selection incident and near-miss rates before and after change.

questions.rationale: Outcome data should show whether the intervention actually reduced the targeted error.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Why should frontline staff participate in learning reviews?

options.text: They can assign blame more easily.
They eliminate the need for data.
They understand how work is actually performed.

questions.rationale: Frontline staff provide practical insight into real workflow, constraints and workarounds.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A medication process depends on remembering six separate verbal steps. Which redesign is BEST?

options.text: Standardise and embed the sequence into workflow or technology.

questions.rationale: Embedding the process reduces reliance on memory and makes safe action easier.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which is an example of a latent system condition?

options.text: A nurse pressing the wrong button.
A confusing electronic display that has existed for months.

questions.rationale: Latent conditions are underlying system weaknesses that may remain hidden until they contribute to an event.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A barcode is repeatedly bypassed because scanners fail. What should leaders conclude?

options.text: The workaround is a signal to investigate equipment reliability and workflow.

questions.rationale: Frequent workarounds often indicate technology or workflow problems that require redesign.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which control best reduces wrong-route administration?
questions.rationale: Engineering controls such as non-interchangeable connectors are stronger than warnings.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: A learning review produces ten recommendations but none have owners. What is the main weakness?

options.text: Recommendations are unlikely to be implemented or monitored.

questions.rationale: Recommendations should be specific, assigned and evaluated.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which finding suggests a control has created an unintended risk?

options.text: Error rates fall but treatment delays increase substantially.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures identify unintended consequences such as harmful delays.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: What is the primary aim of human-factors design?

options.text: Design systems that support normal human limitations.

questions.rationale: Human-factors design recognises limits in attention, memory and perception and supports safer performance.

questions.sectionLabel: Human Factors and Systems Thinking in Medication Error Prevention
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST demonstrates effective system redesign?

options.text: The safer action becomes easier, error rates fall and the improvement is sustained.

questions.rationale: Successful redesign changes the system, reduces error and remains effective over time.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: What is the first step in a medication quality-improvement project?

options.text: Define the specific problem using data.

questions.rationale: Improvement begins by defining the problem and understanding current practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which is an outcome measure?
questions.rationale: Outcome measures show what happened to patients or systems, such as harm rates.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which is a process measure?

options.text: Percentage of medication reconciliations completed on time.

questions.rationale: Process measures show whether recommended care occurred.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Why are balancing measures important?

options.text: They detect unintended effects such as delays or workload burden.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures help determine whether an improvement causes new problems.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: A ward reports frequent hypoglycaemia after insulin. Which change best reflects a focused improvement?

options.text: Link insulin timing with meal availability and add an escalation pathway.

questions.rationale: The intervention addresses the identified process factors and includes a safer response pathway.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: What is pharmacovigilance?

options.text: Monitoring, recognising and reporting adverse medicine effects.

questions.rationale: Pharmacovigilance supports detection of rare, serious or emerging medicine risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Why should suspected adverse reactions be reported even if causation is uncertain?

options.text: Aggregated reports may reveal emerging patterns.

questions.rationale: Pharmacovigilance systems rely on reports to detect possible safety signals.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which nursing action supports antimicrobial stewardship?

options.text: Questioning unnecessary continuation through appropriate channels.

questions.rationale: Nurses support appropriate medicine, dose, route and duration through monitoring, communication and patient education.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which action best supports opioid stewardship?

options.text: Monitor pain, sedation, respiratory status and ongoing need.

questions.rationale: Stewardship balances benefit and harm through assessment and review.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: A quality project reduces errors but doubles medication-round time. What should the team do?

options.text: Review the balancing measure and adapt the intervention.

questions.rationale: The team should evaluate unintended consequences and refine the change.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Why are small tests of change useful?

options.text: They eliminate the need for data.
They allow learning and adaptation before broad implementation.

questions.rationale: Small tests reduce risk and help teams refine interventions.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which data source best identifies a new pattern of medication harm?

options.text: Aggregated incident, adverse-reaction and audit data.

questions.rationale: Multiple data sources can reveal trends and improvement priorities.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: A hospital sees high reconciliation compliance but continued omission errors. What should the team investigate?

options.text: The quality and accuracy of reconciliation, not only completion.

questions.rationale: High completion does not guarantee effective performance; process quality matters.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects medication stewardship?

options.text: Use the right medicine, dose, route and duration.

questions.rationale: Stewardship promotes appropriate, evidence-informed medicine use.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: A new adverse reaction appears across several countries. What is the value of global pharmacovigilance?

options.text: It removes the need for assessment.
It can identify rare signals not visible in one organisation.

questions.rationale: Pooling reports across settings helps detect rare and emerging risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which intervention best supports deprescribing?

options.text: Ask the patient to decide without information.
Review ongoing need, benefit, harm and patient goals with the multidisciplinary team.

questions.rationale: Deprescribing is a structured, patient-centred review of ongoing necessity and risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: What should happen after a successful medication-safety pilot?

options.text: Standardise effective practices, monitor sustainability and adapt before wider spread.

questions.rationale: Successful changes should be embedded, monitored and scaled thoughtfully.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which indicator best measures independent-check reliability?

options.text: Percentage of high-risk doses with a correctly completed independent check.

questions.rationale: The indicator directly measures the intended safety process.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: A stewardship programme tracks antibiotic duration and readmission. Why both?

options.text: One is a process measure and the other helps assess outcomes or unintended effects.

questions.rationale: Using multiple measure types provides a fuller picture of effectiveness and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement, Pharmacovigilance and Medication Stewardship
questions.stem: Which outcome BEST demonstrates effective quality improvement?

options.text: The targeted harm decreased, key processes improved and unintended effects remained acceptable.

questions.rationale: Improvement should show measurable benefit, reliable process change and acceptable balancing outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Medication Safety, Innovation and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: What is automation bias?

options.text: Over-relying on technology recommendations despite conflicting clinical information.

questions.rationale: Automation bias occurs when users trust technology too readily and fail to apply independent judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Medication Safety, Innovation and Global Collaboration
questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates alert fatigue?

options.text: A critical allergy alert prevents prescribing.
Clinicians override many alerts because they are excessive and often irrelevant.
A barcode confirms the correct patient.
